content.title: About
content.content: Colby is a semi‑hard American cheese made from cow's milk. It has a bright orange color, a moderately sharp flavor, and a slightly crumbly texture. The cheese is commonly used in sandwiches, salads, and as a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Colby was first produced in the 19th century in Wisconsin, USA.
The orange hue is achieved by adding annatto, a natural plant pigment.
Colby is often compared to cheddar but is less aged and has a softer texture.
It melts well, making it popular in hot dishes such as macaroni and cheese.
In the United States, Colby ranks among the top ten most consumed semi‑hard cheeses.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Colby provides a good amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The cheese supplies high‑quality animal protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Probiotic cultures
items.content: Like many cheeses, Colby may contain live bacteria that promote gut health.

items.title: Contains phosphorus
items.content: Phosphorus in the cheese helps with energy metabolism and dental health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience gastrointestinal discomfort after consuming Colby.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The cheese contains a fair amount of salt, so individuals with hypertension should monitor portions.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergic reaction to casein, the main milk protein.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Colby is calorie‑dense; excessive intake can contribute to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Colby can be sliced for sandwiches, added to salads, used in casseroles, pizza, and sauces. It is also served as part of a cheese platter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Colby in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. For longer storage it can be frozen, though the texture may become more crumbly.

content.title: About
content.content: Dandelion greens (Taraxacum officinale) are the edible leaves of the common dandelion, often used in cooking after being cooked. The leaves have a mildly bitter, slightly nutty flavor and a tender texture. They are steamed, boiled, sautéed, or added to soups and stews.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dandelion greens grow on almost every continent and are one of the most widely available wild vegetables.
The leaves are rich in vitamins A, C, and K, as well as minerals such as calcium and iron.
Traditionally, dandelion has been used in folk medicine to support liver and gallbladder function.
Raw leaves can be very bitter; cooking reduces bitterness and makes them easier to digest.
Dandelion is often touted as a "future food" because of its high nutrient density and ability to thrive in low‑input agricultural systems.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Calcium and iron in dandelion greens support bone structure and oxygen transport.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Dandelion greens contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Bitterness
items.content: Consuming large amounts can cause a strong bitter taste and may irritate the stomach.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to dandelion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook dandelion greens by steaming, boiling in soups, sautéing with garlic and olive oil, or braising with meat. Before cooking, rinse the leaves thoroughly and trim any tough stems. A quick sauté with a splash of lemon juice brightens the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh dandelion greens in the refrigerator in a perforated bag with a damp paper towel; they keep for 3–5 days. For longer storage, blanch the leaves briefly and freeze them.
